analysis.one_liner: Guarantees most workers up to seven paid sick days a year to use for their own or a family member's health needs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2026 with 156 of 217 House Democrats cosponsoring and no Republicans, and has sat in three House committees since referral with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require most employers, including the federal government and Congress's own offices, to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year. Workers could use that time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, or partner, or to deal with the aftermath of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Employers who already offer equally generous paid leave would not have to change anything. The bill was referred to three House committees and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of workers who do not currently have paid sick leave, especially low-wage workers in food service, retail, and care work. The bill covers private-sector workers at any employer with at least one employee, federal employees, congressional staff, State employees, and rail workers. It also protects workers from being fired, disciplined, or counted against under attendance policies for using sick time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid sick leave, especially low-wage ones

how_it_helps.text: Workers earn 1 hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year, starting from their first day of employment and usable after 60 days [S2].

The time can be used for the worker's own physical or mental illness, injury, or medical and preventive care, or to care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or other close family member in the same circumstances [S2].
It can also be used to recover from or handle domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, including seeking medical attention, counseling, relocation, or taking legal action [S2].

Employers may not fire, discriminate against, or retaliate against workers for using or asking about the rights, may not count sick days against no-fault attendance policies, and may not require workers to find their own replacement [S2].

Enforcement includes a private right of action in federal or state court with attorney's fees, liquidated damages, and Labor Department investigations, and the law covers federal employees, congressional staff, GAO and Library of Congress employees, and rail carriers [S2].
The bill does not override state or local laws that provide more generous sick leave, and employers with policies that already meet the requirements are exempt from adding more [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would fund up to 56 hours of paid time per employee per year. This falls hardest on small businesses and low-margin industries like restaurants, retail, and hospitality, which employ many of the workers who currently lack paid sick leave. Employers already offering equivalent paid leave would see no change.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, especially small businesses in service industries

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost for employers, particularly small businesses and low-margin service industries, which must fund paid time that can reach seven days per employee per year, and some may reduce hiring, hours, or other benefits to offset it [S2].

For absences lasting more than three consecutive workdays, employers may require a health care provider's certification, which can mean an extra doctor's visit for the worker, and documentation requirements for domestic violence leave could be burdensome to produce [S2].

The 56-hour annual cap means the bill sets a floor rather than a generous benefit: unused time carries over but no worker can accrue more than 56 hours in a calendar year, and employers owe nothing for unused sick time when a worker leaves [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers without any paid sick leave, the benefit is direct and large: they stop having to choose between a paycheck and a sick day, or working while contagious. The cost is borne by employers and would be real for small businesses, though the bill accommodates employers that already provide equivalent leave and preserves more generous state laws. The design is straightforward rather than ambitious: it is a floor, not a comprehensive paid leave program.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Education and Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight and Government Reform committees, and no committee or floor action has taken place since.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on February 12, 2026 [S1].
It was referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce and, in addition, to the Committees on House Administration and Oversight and Government Reform [S4].
156 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S3].
As of the latest recorded action, no hearing, markup, or vote has occurred in any of the three committees [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost from an outcome, because no outcome exists. If the bill stays where it is, employers who would have borne the cost of the mandate come out ahead, and workers without paid sick leave remain without it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Still undecided; inaction would favor employers

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 12, 2026, with a broad group of Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee majority
against.what_they_did: Has taken no recorded action on the bill — no hearing or markup — since referral on February 12, 2026.

against.name: U.S. business groups such as the U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.role: Opponents of federal paid leave mandates
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed federal paid sick leave mandates as costs on employers.

sides.party_line_note: All 156 cosponsors are House Democrats and none are Republicans, and Republicans hold the House majority (223 of 441 seats), putting the bill's fate with the opposite party [S3].

industries.industry: Employers in food service, retail, hospitality, and other low-wage service industries
industries.note: These employers would have to fund up to 56 hours of paid sick leave per employee per year, and they employ many of the workers who currently have no paid sick leave. Their cost is those workers' direct gain.

industries.industry: Employers with existing generous paid leave policies
industries.note: Employers whose existing policies already meet the bill's requirements are exempt from providing additional time, so the bill would cost them little while setting a floor that keeps competitors from undercutting them on benefits.
The mandate applies to any employer with one or more employees, so small businesses bear the per-employee cost without large-firm economies of scale.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House and the bill referred to three committees more than four months ago with no recorded action, the bill's most likely path is to remain in committee until the Congress ends, as in previous Congresses where the Healthy Families Act was introduced without receiving a vote. It has essentially no path to the floor absent a change in House control or leadership priorities.
